title: NGC1850 as seen with the Very Large Telescope and Hubble
caption: The star cluster NGC 1850 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope and the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: ESO, NASA/ESA/R. Gilmozzi/S. Casertano, J. Schmidt

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Reddish filaments surround a cluster of thousands of stars in this image. The cluster is NGC 1850, which lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbour of the Milky Way, roughly 160 000 light-years away. The filaments are vast clouds of hydrogen, believed to be the remains of supernova explosions.

The picture overlays two sets of visible-light observations. ESO's Very Large Telescope captured the wide field and the filaments, while the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope imaged the central cluster.

Among its many stars, NGC 1850 hosts a black hole with 11 times the Sun's mass, circled by a star of five solar masses. Astronomers inferred the black hole's presence from the star's orbit, using the MUSE instrument at the VLT. It was the first small black hole beyond the Milky Way to be discovered by this method. Black holes give off no light of their own, so watching how they tug on companions is one of the few ways to find them.
scale: NGC 1850 lies roughly 160 000 light-years away, according to ESO.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light overlay combining FORS1 on the VLT with Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2, including hydrogen-alpha filters. The hydrogen filaments appear reddish, but the full colour mapping isn't published.

understand.eye: The black hole itself is invisible. Its presence was inferred only from the motion of a star around it.

explore: The Large Magellanic Cloud lies in the direction of the constellation Dorado. The filters used include ones that isolate the red glow of hydrogen, on both the VLT's FORS1 instrument and Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2.
